samples.text:
In some countries, people can now use an app on their mobile phone to report a crime and send videos to the police. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although it must be used carefully.

The first advantage is that reporting a crime become much easier and faster. In the past, people had to call the police or go to the police station, and many people did not want to do this because it take a lot of time. With an app, a person who sees a car accident or a theft in the street can send a report in only one minute. As a result, more crimes are reported and police can react more quickly.

The second advantage is that video evidence is very useful. Often, it is difficult for the police to know exactly what happened, because witnesses remember different things. A video clearly shows the person who commit the crime, his face and the time and place. This can help the police to catch criminals and to prove in court that they are guilty.

On the other hand, there are some problems. Some people may send false reports about neighbours they do not like, or they may film innocent people and put them in trouble. Also, if people try to film a dangerous situation, they can put themselves in danger. Moreover, the police may receive too many small reports and not have time for serious crimes.

In conclusion, I think crime reporting apps are a positive development because they make reporting easier and give the police good evidence. However, the police should check all reports carefully and tell people not to take risks for filming.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas with some support but limited depth · mechanical linking (The first, The second, On the other hand) · adequate vocabulary · tense and agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Several countries have introduced mobile phone apps that allow citizens to report crimes and upload photographs or video evidence directly to the police. I believe this is a positive development, as it makes reporting easier and can improve the effectiveness of policing.

The main benefit is that it removes many of the barriers that discourage people from reporting crimes. Calling the police or visiting a station can be time-consuming and intimidating, so many minor offences, such as vandalism or dangerous driving, are simply never reported. An app allows a witness to submit a report within minutes, and even anonymously in some cases. This gives the police a more accurate picture of where and when crimes happen, which can help them decide where to send patrols.

Video evidence can also strengthen investigations. Eyewitness memories are often incomplete, particularly after a stressful event, whereas a recording captures details such as appearances, vehicle registration numbers and the order of events. This kind of evidence can help identify suspects more quickly and may also protect innocent people who have been wrongly accused.

Nevertheless, there are some risks to consider. Some users might submit false or malicious reports, and there are concerns about privacy when members of the public film others without permission. There is also a danger that people put themselves at risk by stopping to record a violent incident instead of moving to safety. However, these problems can be managed if the police verify all reports carefully and the app clearly advise users never to endanger themselves.

In conclusion, although crime-reporting apps must be carefully managed, they encourage more people to report offences and provide valuable evidence. For these reasons, I consider them a positive development in the fight against crime.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · main ideas extended with specific examples · risks acknowledged and answered · well-organised with varied cohesion · good vocabulary (intimidating, malicious) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Police forces in a number of countries now allow members of the public to report offences through smartphone apps, attaching photographs or video footage as evidence. While such tools raise legitimate concerns about privacy and misuse, I consider them, on the whole, a positive development.

Their chief merit is that they make reporting crime far more accessible. Many offences go unreported not because witnesses are indifferent but because the process seems disproportionately burdensome: waiting on the phone, visiting a station or giving a lengthy statement for an incident that may appear minor. By reducing reporting to a few taps, apps capture offences that would otherwise disappear from official records, such as antisocial behaviour, fly-tipping or reckless driving. Better data, in turn, allows police to identify patterns and deploy their limited resources more intelligently.

Footage recorded at the scene can also be valuable evidence. Human memory is notoriously unreliable, especially under stress, while a timestamped video preserves details that witnesses may later forget or misremember. Such material can accelerate investigations and, just as importantly, can exonerate people who have been wrongly suspected.

The risks, however, deserve careful attention. An easy reporting channel may be exploited to harass neighbours or settle personal disputes, and the circulation of footage of identifiable individuals raises obvious privacy concerns. There is also a danger that the desire to record encourages bystanders to film incidents instead of seeking safety or offering help. These problems are serious but manageable: reports can be screened by trained staff, footage can be restricted to police use, and users can be clearly instructed to prioritise their own safety.

In conclusion, crime-reporting apps enable the public to contribute more effectively to their own security and supply the police with better intelligence. Provided that robust safeguards accompany them, they represent a welcome step forward.
samples.why: Clear, qualified positive judgement · ideas developed with precise reasoning and examples · risks evaluated with realistic safeguards · skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (exonerate, fly-tipping) · error-free, varied structures.
